title-group.article-title: Factors influencing unplanned readmission within 30 days in patients with heart failure and their predictive value: a prospective study

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Heart failure imposes a significant healthcare burden, with early unplanned readmissions post-discharge linked to poor outcomes. Identifying risk factors and their predictive value is crucial for targeted interventions.

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: To investigate gender differences in cumulative hazard function and the factors influencing 30-day unplanned readmissions in heart failure patients, and to compare their predictive value.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A prospective study of heart failure patients hospitalized in Beijing Hospital from October 2023 to March 2024. Patients’ nutritional status was assessed using the Mini-Nutritional Assessment Scale Short Version (MNA-SF), frailty was evaluated using the Groningen Frailty Index (GFI), and the Appendicular Skeletal Muscle Mass Index (ASMI) was calculated. Multifactorial Cox regression analysis was conducted, and ROC curves were plotted for predictive modeling.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of 121 heart failure patients (60.3% males), aged (69.87 ± 11.9) years were included. With a median follow-up duration of 30 days, 25 (20.7%) patients with readmission. COX regression analysis stratified by gender showed that age, regular smoking, nutritional status, left ventricular ejection fraction(LVEF), brain natriuretic peptide(BNP), GFI, and ASMI were independent predictors of readmission within 30 days in patients with heart failure (P < 0.050). ROC curve analysis showed that age, BNP, ASMI, smoking status, LVEF, nutritional status, and GFI individually as well as in combination predicted readmission within 30 days in patients with heart failure; the joint model performed optimally, with an AUC value reaching 0.877 (95%CI 0.801 ∼ 0.952, P < 0.001), with a sensitivity of 0.920 and a specificity of 0.729.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: A multifactorial approach including age, BNP, ASMI, smoking status, LVEF, nutritional status, and GFI predicts 30-day readmission risk, offering a basis for clinical intervention strategies to improve patient outcomes.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome characterized by high morbidity, mortality, and rehospitalization rates, and has become a major global public health problem due to its increasing socioeconomic burden, especially in the context of accelerated aging [1]. According to the latest large-scale epidemiological data, the prevalence of stage A heart failure and stage B heart failure in the general population aged ≥ 35 years is 35.8% and 42.8%, respectively, and is the main cause of cardiovascular mortality in China [2, 3]. Readmission is a recognized indicator used to measure the quality of care and outcomes of heart failure patients. Previous foreign systematic evaluations have shown that the 30-day readmission rate of heart failure patients is around 20%, and has risen in recent years; whereas data on 30-day readmission for heart failure in China are scarce, a retrospective study showed that readmission occurs within 30 days for about 22.8% of heart failure patients [4, 5]. Frequent readmissions seriously affects patients’ prognosis and quality of life and need to be controlled or avoided by early risk identification and intervention [6–8]. However, it’s widely acknowledged that predicting the rate of unplanned readmissions in heart failure patients is more challenging than predicting mortality rates, because unplanned readmissions may be the result of a complex interplay between clinical disease factors, psychological behaviors, and socioenvironmental influences [9, 10]. Meanwhile, with the increasing research on risk factors for cardiovascular events, the results of previous studies on factors influencing short-term readmission in hospitalized heart failure patients have lagged significantly. For example, recent studies have shown that decreased skeletal muscle mass, an important manifestation of sarcopenia, is a key factor in the progression of heart failure, and that heart failure patients with comorbid muscle atrophy have a worse prognosis [11]; the presence of frailty significantly increases the incidence of poor prognosis in heart failure patients, but previous assessments of weakness have mostly been limited to physical aspects, ignoring psychological and cognitive dimensions of the decline [12–14]. Therefore, the purpose of this study is to investigate gender differences in cumulative hazard function, analyze the influencing factors of 30-day unplanned readmission in heart failure patients after discharge and their predictive value, subsequently to construct a predictive model, from which we can identify heart failure patients at high risk of readmission and explore non-pharmacological interventions to improve short-term outcomes.

sec.title: Study design and population
sec.p: This prospective longitudinal study consecutively recruited heart failure patients who were hospitalized in the Department of Cardiovascular Medicine of Beijing Hospital from September 2023 to March 2024 for the study. According to the estimation of rate and hypothesis testing formula while considering the 15% loss of visit rate, the final calculation was made to get the required sample size of at least 104 cases. Inclusion criteria: (1) meeting the diagnostic criteria for heart failure in the National Heart Failure Guidelines 2018 [15]; (2) age ≥ 18 years; (3) willingness to participate and cooperate, and sign the informed consent. Exclusion criteria: (1) those with combined psychiatric diseases or significant cognitive and language dysfunction; (2) those with combined tumors and other serious diseases such as heart, lung and liver; (3) pregnant patients. A total of 121 patients with heart failure were finally enrolled in the study. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Beijing Hospital (approval number: 2023BJYYEC-356-01). Clinical trial number: not applicable.

sec.title: Investigation content
sec.p: (1) General information. It mainly includes age, gender, smoking status, drinking history, cardiac function grading etc. (2) Nutritional status. The short version of Mini Nutrition Assessment-SF (MNA-SF) developed by Laurence et al. in 2001 was used, which is suitable for the Chinese hospitalized population [16]. The scale consists of 6 entries, including whether the patient has lost appetite in the past three months, whether he/she has lost weight, mobility, whether he/she has been traumatized or acutely ill in the past three months, psychopathology, and body mass index (BMI) or calf circumference. A score of 12–14 is considered normal nutrition status, 8–11 is considered at risk of malnutrition, and 0–7 is considered malnourished [17]. (3) Frailty status. The Groningen Frailty Index (GFI) was used. The scale consists of 15 entries and includes 3 dimensions: 9 somatic (mobility, multiple health problems, physical fatigue, vision, hearing), 1 cognitive (cognitive functioning), and 5 psychosocial (emotional isolation, depressed mood, and feelings of anxiety). GFI scores ranging from 0 to 15 reflect a range from healthy to severely debilitated, with a score of greater than 4 being in a state of debilitation [18]. (4) Appendicular Skeletal Muscle Mass Index (ASMI). An anthropometric formula validated for large-scale populations was used to calculate the patient’s ASM as follows:

Weight, height and age are expressed in kilograms, centimeters and years, respectively; for gender, it is coded as 1 for males and 2 for females [19, 20]. ASMI is expressed as ASM/height in squared meters, with ASMI < 7.05 kg/m2 for men or < 5.63 kg/m2 for women as reduced skeletal muscle mass [21]. (5) Grip strength. Grip strength was measured with an electronic grip strength meter on the dominant hand and non-dominant hand, and a grip strength of < 28 kg for men or < 18 kg for women was considered to be reduced grip strength. All tools used in this study are publicly available.

sec.title: Observation indicators
sec.p: (1) Baseline information. This includes age, gender, blood pressure, heart rate, smoking history, drinking history, New York Heart Association (NYHA) Class, left ventricular ejection fraction(LVEF), ASMI, grip strength, blood sodium, blood potassium, brain natriuretic peptide(BNP), estimated glomerular filtration rate(eGFR), comorbidities, information on medication use, nutritional status, GFI. (2) Readmission within 30 days. For patients who were readmitted within 30 days, the duration and reason for the patient’s hospitalization were recorded; for patients who were not admitted to the department within 30 days, the patients were asked by telephone around the 35th day after their discharge whether there had been any readmission during that period and the reason for the readmission.

sec.title: Sample size
sec.p: We used PASS 2021 for the calculation of the required sample size. In the software, we navigated to “Survival” and subsequently selected “Cox Regression” for our analysis. Based on the findings of Foroutan et al. [22]. and Poon et al. [23]., we set the Event Rate to 0.25 and the R-Squared to 0.7, with all other parameters retaining their default values. This process yielded a sample size estimate of 103. Subsequently, we proceeded to select the “ROC” option, referencing the study by Zheng et al. [24]for parameter settings. This approach resulted in a sample size estimate of 107. To ensure the robustness of our study, we integrated the outcomes from both methodologies and opted for the higher figure. Furthermore, considering a dropout rate of 10%, we determined the minimum required sample size for our study to be 118 cases.

sec.title: Quality control methods
sec.p: The study subjects were selected from the patients admitted to the hospital in strict accordance with the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Within 2 days after the patients were admitted to the hospital, general status and disease-related information was collected through the inpatient electronic medical record system; nutritional assessment and grip strength measurement were performed by one trained investigator, and the completed case report forms were checked by two investigators. The study was fully communicated to the study participants and their families before the start of the investigation, and the informed consent form was signed by the study participants.

sec.title: Statistical methods
sec.p: SPSS25.0 and R Studio 4.2.3 were used for data analysis. Measurement data conforming to normal distribution were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (‾χ ± s), and t-test was used for comparison between groups; count data not conforming to normal distribution were expressed as median and quartiles [M(P25, P75)], and rank sum test was used for comparison between groups. Count data were expressed as frequencies or percentages (%), and comparisons between groups were performed using theχ2 test. Because the results of 30-day readmission rates in previous studies differed between genders, this study was stratified by gender in the multifactorial analysis [25]. Differential variables were incorporated into the final predictive model by univariate analysis and multifactorial COX proportional risk modeling, and subject work characteristic curves (ROCs) were plotted and areas under the curve (AUCs) were calculated. Appropriate packages in R Studio 4.2.3 were uesd to conduct interaction tests and calculate the C-statistic of the Cox proportional hazards model. P < 0.05 was considered a statistically significant difference.

sec.title: Comparison of patients’ baseline data
sec.p: During a median follow-up duration of (30 ± 8.17) days, 25 (20.7%) patients experienced initial unplanned readmissions within 30 days, and the rest of the patients (96, 79.3%) did not have readmission events.There was no statistically significant difference in the comparison of gender, history of alcohol consumption, grip strength, blood sodium and potassium between the two groups of the readmission group and the non-readmission group (P > 0.05); age, smoking history, LVEF, BNP, ASMI, nutritional status and GFI were compared with statistically significant differences (P < 0.05)(Table 1).

sec.title: Multifactorial COX proportional model analysis of unplanned readmissions within 30 days in patients with heart failure
sec.p: Influential factors with statistically significant differences in univariate analysis of heart failure patients, including age, BNP, ASMI, smoking status, LVEF, nutritional status, and GFI were jointly included in the COX proportional risk model and stratified by gender, and the results showed that all of them were independent influences on unplanned readmission within 30 days in patients with heart failure (P < 0.05), as shown in Table 2. The cumulative survival risk graph stratified by gender showed that male patients had a higher risk of 30-day readmission compared to females, with Log-rank testχ2 = 4.35, P = 0.037(Fig. 1). The interaction analysis indicated that there was no interaction between gender and the other covariates(Fig. 2). The C-statistics and − 2 Log Likelihood of this model composed of these factors were 0.851 and 159.65.

sec.title: ROC curves for unplanned readmissions in heart failure patients within 30 days of hospital discharge
sec.p: Based on the results of multifactorial COX regression analysis and previous studies, we constructed ROC curves to predict unplanned readmissions in heart failure patients within 30 days of discharge, and the results showed that the AUCs of age, BNP, ASMI, regular smoking or not, LVEF, nutritional status, and GFI individually and in combination predicted unplanned readmission within 30 days of patients with heart failure, respectively, were 0.677 (95% CI 0.556 ∼ 0.797, P = 0.007), 0.364 (95% CI 0.238 ∼ 0.490, P = 0.036), 0.698 (95% CI 0.568 ∼ 0.829, P = 0.002), 0.647 (95% CI 0.516 ∼ 0.778, P = 0.024), 0.190 (95% CI 0.097 ∼ 0.283, P < 0.001), 0.660 (95%CI 0.532 ∼ 0.789, P = 0.014), 0.747 (95%CI 0.636 ∼ 0.857, P < 0.001), and 0.877 (95%CI 0.801 ∼ 0.952, P < 0.001), and the Youden exponent of the combined model was 0.649, corresponding to a sensitivity of 0.920 and a specificity of 0.729(Fig. 3). Table 3 shows the results of DeLong test between the combined model and individual models.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: With the global population aging, the incidence of various cardiovascular-related chronic diseases is on the rise, and heart failure is the end stage of the cardiovascular chain of events. Frequent readmission of patients with heart failure is significantly associated with higher mortality rates, while relatively fewer studies have been conducted on readmission of patients with heart failure in China, and past measures relying on medication have not led to significant improvements in the risk of readmission and the poor prognosis [26]. Some multidisciplinary disease management programs have a positive effect, but they may lead to an increase in the cost of treatment [27]. Therefore, non-pharmacologic disease management interventions are considered to be more cost-effective and can significantly improve patient self-care and prognostic quality, including reducing readmission risks [28]. The results of this study showed that the incidence of 30-day unplanned readmission was significantly high in patients with heart failure, and patient age, BNP, ASMI, regular smoking or not, LVEF, nutritional status, and GFI were the independent influencing factors; among them, targeted non-pharmacological interventions can be proposed on the basis of scientific assessment of the nutritional, debilitating, and skeletal muscle mass decline. The model constructed from above variables had a good predictive value of the risk of readmission.

The 30-day unplanned readmission rate in this study was 20.66%, which was slightly lower than those reported in previous literature, probably due to the exclusion of some planned admissions as well as differences in sample size and source [29]. Frequent readmissions not only affects the quality of life of heart failure patients, but also aggravate the economic burden on families and society, so an in-depth discussion of the influencing factors of readmission in heart failure patients from multiple perspectives is conducive to accurately identifying high-risk patients and formulating personalized intervention strategies to improve the quality of life of the patients and to reduce the cost of health care [28–30].

Age is an important demographic factor influencing the prognostic quality for a number of chronic diseases, including heart failure [31]. Studies have shown that the incidence of all-cause readmission in heart failure patients increases with age, with the risk of all-cause readmission in heart failure patients ≥ 65 and ≥ 80 years of age being 3.3 and 4.1 times higher than that in patients under 65 years of age, respectively [32]. Smoking is also a well-established cardiovascular risk factor [33]. In this study, age and regular smoking had a significant effect on 30-day unplanned readmission in patients with heart failure and had an important predictive value, which suggests the need to pay close attention to the progression of the disease in elderly patients in the clinical work, to educate patients with heart failure who currently smoke, to emphasize the effects of tobacco use on cardiac function and overall health status, and encourage them to actively quit smoking; in the period of preparation for hospital discharge, Enhance health education and continuity of care for the patients themselves and their families.

In this study, no interaction was found between gender and other variables in this study, but the cumulative risk of 30-day unplanned readmission was higher in males compared to females. Many cohort studies have shown that females have a lower risk of cardiovascular-related death or hospitalization due to heart failure compared to males [34, 35].Our study suggests that gender may not be an independent risk factor affecting survival time, and gender differences in the model may be explained by other factors, because the estrogens has a protective effect on heart function; additionally, females tend to exhibit a better responsiveness to vasoactive drugs and generally have stronger social support than males [35–37].Variables such as LVEF and BNP in the COX model effectively reflect and explain this protective effect. However, a systematic review by Hoang et al. has pointed out that there are still contradictory results regarding this issue [25]. Therefore, the mechanism of gender difference in heart failure has not completely been evaluated. The effect of gender on the occurrence of short-term readmissions in heart failure patients needs to be further analyzed after more careful differentiation based on the characteristics of the study population.

LVEF and BNP levels are traditionally recognized important indicators of heart failure severity, and both were independent risk factors for 30-day unplanned readmission in patients with heart failure in the present study, consistent with previous findings [38–40]. However, BNP was a poor independent predictor of readmission in the present study, in contrast to previous studies [41, 42]. It’s probably due to the fact that there were more missing BNP data in our study, which may still lead to the discrepancy between the analyzed results and the real situation, although reasonable interpolation was performed during data processing. Additionally, the BNP data were measured at patient admission. Somma et al. [43] have suggested that the timing of BNP measurement may influence its predictive value. In contrast, previous studies supporting the predictive value of BNP for readmission have followed up for more than 30 days, with outcome measures primarily focused on various cardiac events. In contrast, this study used short-term (30-day) unplanned readmission events as the outcome measure [41, 44]. Therefore, the level of BNP and its trajectory may be more valuable for long-term prognosis in heart failure patients, particularly for cardiovascular-related adverse events. Some studies have also found that, similar to the results of this study, the predictive value for heart failure patient outcomes is higher when BNP is combined with other indicators than when BNP is used alone [45]. The predictive value of BNP for short-term readmission events in heart failure patients requires further discussion in larger sample sizes. LVEF showed the poorest performance in this study in terms of readmission risk prediction. Yu et al. [46] found that LVEF exhibits a U-shaped relationship with prognosis in heart failure patients, that high LVEF does not indicate a low risk of adverse events such as readmission in heart failure patients, and that 60–65% may be the range with the lowest prognostic risk in heart failure patients but the gender may have an influence. Additionally, patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) experience a significant decline in LVEF. However, in clinical practice, HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) or heart failure with improved ejection fraction (HFimpEF) are more commonly observed. These patients do not experience a notable decrease in LVEF, but this does not indicate a better prognosis. This complex relationship between LVEF and prognosis in heart failure patients may therefore be an important factor influencing the predictive value of LVEF in this study. This feature suggests that the prognostic significance of LVEF should be interpreted cautiously in clinical practice and that it needs to be applied in combination with other indicators, rather than simply judging according to ultrasound results, to avoid misjudging the prognostic risk of certain patients.

In this study, nutritional status was an independent predictive risk factor for unplanned readmission within 30 days in heart failure patients, and the risk of readmission in malnourished patients was over six times higher than that in patients with normal nutritional status, which is consistent with the results of the Lim et al. [47]. Previous studies have shown that heart failure patients have poor dietary quality and poor control of sodium intake, particularly among males, those with lower education levels, and those with low income, which can lead to the worsening of heart failure [48, 49]. In comparison, female patients tend to have healthier dietary patterns, so the nutritional status may also partially reflect and explain the impact of gender on overall survival risks [50, 51]. Nutritional status can be improved by health education and dietary guidance during hospitalization and during the pre-discharge period [26].

ASMI is an important indicator of skeletal muscle content and diagnosis of sarcopenia. The results of this study showed that ASMI was a protective factor for unplanned readmission within 30 days in patients with heart failure and had the high individual predictive value with an AUC value of 0.698. The underlying mechanisms by which ASMI affects the prognosis of patients with heart failure include disorders of protein anabolism and hormonal balance, apoptosis, oxidative stress, and inflammation [52, 53]. The gold standard for ASMI measurement is magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT), and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) or bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) are also widely used in clinical research, but the above methods have limitations such as high cost, radiation exposure, and poor reliability, which make it difficult to promote the determination of ASMI in the clinic and thus affect the assessment of the patient’s prognostic risk, so we employed the anthropometric ASM equation model to calculate the ASMI in the present study. An anthropometric ASM equation model was used in this study to calculate ASMI in patients with heart failure, which has been validated and applied on a large scale in the Chinese population, and shows strong agreement with DXA [19–21]. Our study showed that the ASMI calculated by anthropometric equation has high predictive value for the occurrence of 30-day unplanned readmission in heart failure patients.

Frailty is a common comorbidity in elderly patients with heart failure [54]. Frailty increases the symptom burden in heart failure patients, who usually face a greater risk of adverse prognosis such as readmission and death and have a poorer quality of life than the average patient [55–57]. The Fried or FRAIL scale was mainly used in previous studies, which can only assess frailty in physical functioning, whereas the GFI used in this study is more complex, covers multiple dimensions such as physical, psychological, and social functioning, and provides a more objective and comprehensive assessment of frailty. The results of the study indicate that patients assessed as “problematic or dependent” and “frailty” by the GFI had a risk of 30-day unplanned readmission that was respectively more than 6 and 10 times higher than that of other patients, and the GFI had the highest predictive value of the variables individually. This suggests that clinicians or nurses should use a comprehensive tool to assess the frailty of patients with heart failure. In addition to physical frailty, they should also pay attention to the patient’s mental, psychological, and social frailty. It is recommended that the assessment and intervention of frailty be incorporated into the routine care of patients with heart failure. Currently, there are a variety of scales for the assessment of frailty, but the most appropriate scale for clinical heart failure patients is not yet clear, and future in-depth exploration is needed to study the best specialized tool to improve the quality of frailty assessment in heart failure patients.

At present, no models are currently recommended for clinical practice due to their complexity or unreliable performance. The “one-size-fits-all” approach—encompassing as much of the national population and potential risk factors as possible, can undermine the model’s simplicity and interpretability [58–60]. Given that there is no significant difference in performance between machine learning models and traditional statistical models, we extracted objective data from clinical medical systems, while subjective data were obtained by professionals using scales to conduct face-to-face assessments with patients, and attempted to tailor risk factors to construct a more sensitive readmission risk model, employing the COX proportional hazards model and the ROC curve [61]. The final combined prediction model includes objective indicators and subjective indicators, demonstrating good reliability, simplicity, and interpretability.

Looking ahead, future research should focus on developing and validating predictive models that incorporate these risk factors to enhance the precision of readmission risk assessment. There is also a need for studies that evaluate the impact of targeted interventions on readmission rates and patient outcomes. Furthermore, research should investigate the role of emerging biomarkers and digital health technologies in improving the management of heart failure patients. Ultimately, these efforts should contribute to the development of more effective strategies for preventing readmissions and enhancing the quality of life for heart failure patients.

There are several limitations and biases in our study. Firstly, the study’s generalizability is constrained by its single-center design and relatively small sample size, which may not fully capture the heterogeneity of heart failure patients across different healthcare settings. Secondly, the study did not distinguish between the subtypes of heart failure, which could influence the impact of certain risk factors. Thirdly, the reliance on some missing data, which was addressed through imputation, may introduce some degree of bias or uncertainty into the findings. Lastly, while the study employed a comprehensive approach to risk factor assessment, the cross-sectional nature of the data collection limits the ability to establish causality or temporality in the observed associations. Future research with larger, multicenter cohorts and longitudinal data is required to validate and expand upon these findings. Additionally, the study employed convenience sampling, which may not capture a representative sample of the broader heart failure population. Participants selected by convenience might differ from the general patient population in unmeasured characteristics, leading to a potential selection bias; and the use of various tools and scales may introduce measurement bias due to variability in the application of these instruments and inter-rater reliability.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Our investigation revealed that male patients had a higher risk of 30-day readmission compared to the females. Age, BNP, ASMI, regular smoking, LVEF, nutritional status, and GFI are the influencing factors of 30-day unplanned readmission after discharge of heart failure patients, and the prediction model jointly constructed based on the above five indicators has good differentiation and clinical practicability. The necessity for further prospective studies with large sample sizes remains essential.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: The datasets generated and analyzed during the current study are not publicly accessible due to ethical restrictions aimed at protecting the privacy of research participants. However, de-identified data can be made available upon reasonable request to the corresponding author, subject to compliance with institutional data sharing agreements and ethical review requirements.
